$comment: THE HOSTNAME RULE'S CASES, AND THE ONE PLACE THE VERDICTS ARE DECIDED.
App\Features\Landing\PublishedSite::HOSTNAME_PATTERN is the rule. It is mirrored into
so apps/site can refuse a hostile `Host` with the same rule the publisher refuses it with
(ADR-005). The two files therefore hold the same characters -- but PCRE and ECMAScript are
different dialects, and holding the same characters is not speaking the same language.
This file is the measurement. PublishedSiteKeyMirrorTest drives every case below through
the PHP rule and site-keys.test.ts drives the same cases through the TypeScript one, each
asserting the `safe` value recorded here. NEITHER TEST DECIDES A VERDICT: if the two
engines ever disagree about a case, one of them goes red and the case names itself.
Hand-curated rather than generated, deliberately -- a generated case list would be
generated by one of the two engines and would therefore agree with it by construction.
The cases cover every construct the pattern uses (anchors, character classes, groups, `?`,
`+`) plus the inputs a `Host` header can actually carry: ports, trailing dots, upper case,
traversal, newlines, and the length boundary in both directions.

cases.why: the ordinary shape: two lower-case labels
single-character labels are legal DNS and legal here
more than two labels
an interior hyphen
a label may start with a digit
all-digit labels
one label: the pattern's `+` requires at least one dot group
empty
a bare dot has no label on either side
the traversal segment itself, which is why this rule runs before any key is built
a trailing dot is valid in DNS and is NOT a key we write, so it is refused rather than trimmed
a leading dot
an empty interior label
a label may not start with a hyphen
a label may not end with a hyphen
the same rule on a later label
upper case: the key layout is lower-case only, so this is refused rather than folded
all upper case
a port, which a `Host` header carries routinely -- the caller strips it before asking
traversal through a slash: the case that would read outside the host's own prefix
a path
a scheme-relative authority
a scheme
a trailing newline -- anchored at both ends, so `$` cannot be satisfied before it
header injection shape
a space
an underscore is not in the character class
a NUL byte
a wildcard: a certificate concept, never a key
an IPv4 literal passes the rule, and that is deliberate -- it is a well-formed key segment and the DNS CHECK constraint upstream is what decides whether a tenant may claim it
an IPv6 literal in `Host` form: brackets are not in the character class
punycode is plain ASCII and passes, which is how an internationalised domain reaches a key

non-ASCII is refused unencoded -- and this is the case that proves PHP's byte count and JavaScript's code-unit count cannot change a verdict, because the pattern rejects it whichever number the length check saw

lengthCases.label: at the boundary
lengthCases.why: 253 characters exactly -- HOSTNAME_MAX_LENGTH is inclusive. Counted, not estimated: the first draft of this case said a{247} and that is 252

lengthCases.label: one over
lengthCases.why: 254 characters: refused by the length check, never reaching the regex
